↳ Posted by ceolachan on July 11th, 2008.

Well, as it appears as “Lady Harriet Hope” in 18th century collections - and it seems that Lady Hope was the Lady of Hopetoun, by the Firth of Forth, I’d suggest that you don’t take O’Neill’s as gospel.

↳ Posted by Weejie on February 17th, 2013.

You’ll read elsewhere that:

[Lady Harriet/Harriot Hope has been identified (by Jerry O’Sullivan & Brian McCandless) as Lady Henrietta Johnstone (1682-1750), married to the Charles Hope (1681-1742), 1st Earl of Hopetoun in 1699. ]

I’m not totally convinced. The family is very likely, but “Lady Henrietta Johnstone” also had a daughter who was a “Lady Henrietta Hope” (1706-1745, later becoming Lady Henrietta Napier) , and a granddaughter with the same name (c.1750–1786). The latter (who would have been known under the title even as a child) was known for her religious exploits. All would likely have been called Harriet.

The earliest known publications of the tune (c 1759) could tally with any one of the three, and there is nothing to confirm the dedication.

↳ Posted by Weejie on February 17th, 2013.

Lady Harriet Hope, X:6

Here is the slightly different version published by James Aird in his “Selection of Scotch, English, Irish and Foreign Airs”, vol. 2, Glasgow, n.d. [1785], p. 38, no 104, as “Lady Harriot Hope”.

↳ Posted by Moxhe on October 20th, 2015.

Re: Lady Forbes

@dlowder The fact that it is in O‘Neills tells you that it was in circulation among the Irish music community of Chicago around the turn of the 20th Century. You might consider that alone to qualify it as ’Irish’, but it tells you nothing of its earlier origins. A good number of the reels (and some jigs also) being played at that time would have had Scottish origins – the reel as a dance and musical form came to Ireland from Scotland in the late 18th Century and, whilst many reels have been composed (or have evolved) in Ireland since, the earliest ones in Ireland would have been direct imports – many of which are still current in some form.
